comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## HOW TO SETTLE AC1 — and why the obvious route does NOT work yet

AC1 asks whether DC 8.17.1 returns success or an error for a sub-task `PUT fields.parent` that does
not take effect. The obvious route — read the `bridge_alerts` records that change 1305 now writes on
every `set_parent` failure arm — **does not work in the harness today**, and I confirmed that rather
than assuming it:

    grep -rn "bridge_alert" tests/external/live_jira_dc/                    -> nothing
    grep -rn "bridge_alerts" .github/workflows/external-integration.yml     -> nothing

`record_parent_divergence` writes to `<repo_root>/bridge_state/bridge_alerts/<date>.jsonl` in the
ephemeral runner's working repo. Nothing reads it and nothing uploads it, so the file dies with the
runner. **An absence of alerts in a harness run is therefore NOT evidence that DC returned success** —
it only means nobody looked. Recording this explicitly because the inverse inference is tempting and
would be the same shape of mistake this epic has already paid for twice.

### Three ways to get the observation, cheapest first

 1. **Read the alert store inside the failing cell.** The cell already has the working repo path
    (`dc_store_copy_repo`); after the outbound pass it can glob
    `bridge_state/bridge_alerts/*.jsonl` and assert on the records. Smallest change, no workflow
    edit, and it makes the distinction an ASSERTION rather than a log a human has to read.
 2. **Probe the platform directly**, bypassing rebar entirely: `PUT /rest/api/2/issue/{subtask}`
    with a new parent over raw REST, capture the HTTP status and body, then re-read
    `fields.parent`. This answers the platform question in isolation and does not depend on any
    rebar code path being correct — worth doing FIRST, because if DC returns 400 the whole
    accept-and-ignore reading collapses and option 1 becomes unnecessary.
 3. Dump/upload the alert directory as a workflow artifact. Most general, but it makes the evidence
    something a human must go and read instead of something the suite asserts, so it is the weakest
    of the three despite being the most reusable.

Option 2 then option 1 is the order I would take: establish the platform fact with a direct probe,
then encode whichever answer it gives as an assertion in the cell so it cannot regress silently.

### A follow-on worth noting

Whichever option is taken, the underlying gap is general: rebar's only operator-visible signal for a
swallowed mutation failure is invisible to the very suite built to catch swallowed mutation failures.
Every bug in this family (d067, 8d68, 751e, 2b16, 88d9, 39c1, and this one) was a silent success. A
harness that cannot see the silence-breaking channel will keep needing per-bug forensics.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## CORRECTION TO MY OWN PLAN: the alert store CANNOT settle AC1 for these cells

My earlier comment offered three routes and said option 1 (read the `bridge_alerts` store inside the
failing cell) was the cheapest, with option 2 (a raw-REST probe) worth doing first. **Option 1 does
not work here at all**, and recommending it would have built exactly the vacuous oracle this epic
keeps producing.

### The call graph, traced

`record_parent_divergence` — the write path I was counting on — is invoked from **exactly one
place**: `dispatch_one._update_one`, wrapping the `client.set_parent` call the RECONCILER'S OWN
DISPATCH LOOP makes during a differ-driven pass (`dispatch_one.py:551-601`).

Both live sub-task cells call `dc_transport.set_parent(child, second)` **DIRECTLY**, not through a
pass. Their own docstrings say why: the outbound emit gate (bug 8b25) never emits a parent-field
mutation for a non-epic parent, so the pass-level round-trip is structurally unreachable on DC and
the cells deliberately assert against the transport instead.

**So `record_parent_divergence` is never invoked by either cell, whatever DC does.** Reading
`bridge_alerts` afterwards returns `[]` whether DC errored, silently ignored the write, or the field
actually moved. A "no alert" reading would prove only that the mutation bypassed the reconciler —
precisely the "silence is not a signal" mistake I corrected once already on 39c1, reappearing one
level down.

### What this changes

**Option 2 (raw REST probe) is not merely cheaper — it is the ONLY route that can settle AC1 for
these two cells**, because it depends on no rebar code path being on the route. And it needs no new
plumbing: the `dc_request` fixture already supports `method="PUT"` with a `payload`
(`conftest.py:81-117`).

Concretely, in `test_outbound_set_subtask_parent_round_trips` (and the inbound twin at :1301): before
the existing `set_parent` call, issue a direct `PUT fields.parent` and capture `(status, body)`. A
2xx with an unchanged read-back is **accept-and-ignore**; a 4xx is **rejection**. That is AC1's
question, answered with the raw response, independent of rebar.

Worth pairing with the two cheap falsifiers recorded on [rebar:37e7-d751-0042-4b94]: read
`/rest/api/2/issue/{subtask}/editmeta` for the operations `parent` actually exposes, and compare the
`update`-verb form's error to the `fields` form's.

### The alert-store helper is still worth building — for [rebar:18a5-2bd8-3e56-4bd8], not here

A designed `assert_bridge_alert_for_mutation(repo, cp, ...)` helper in `_dc_support.py` (510 LOC, ~290
of headroom) does have a real payoff on 18a5, whose cell DOES run a real pass and therefore does
reach `record_backstop_failure`. Two properties matter and are worth stating so a future
implementation keeps them:

 * **It takes the pass's `CompletedProcess` as a REQUIRED argument** and asserts `returncode == 0`
   and no traceback BEFORE interpreting the store. Without that, an absent alert directory is
   indistinguishable from a clean pass that wrote nothing — `alert_store.append` creates the
   directory only when it first writes (`alert_store.py:117-119`), so filesystem state alone cannot
   tell "DC succeeded" from "nobody looked".
 * **On 18a5's cell it is diagnostic either way**: an alert found surfaces the specific swallowed
   exception (that ticket's open question); NO alert on a provably-clean pass is a *stronger* result
   — it would mean the create was never attempted, moving 18a5 from stage 3 back to stage 1/2.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## THE PLATFORM PROBE IS UP — Gerrit 1320, and it settles AC1 without depending on any rebar path

Two helpers in `_dc_support.py`, wired into BOTH sub-task parent cells (outbound and inbound):
 * `probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, key, new_parent, *, verb="fields"|"update")` — a raw REST
   PUT bypassing pycontribs entirely, capturing the HTTP status and body `dc_transport.set_parent`
   never surfaces;
 * `probe_subtask_parent_editmeta_ops(dc_request, key)` — reads which operations DC actually exposes
   on `parent`, one of the two falsifiers recorded on [rebar:37e7-d751-0042-4b94].

Both verb forms are probed, which is the other falsifier: if `{"update":{"parent":[{"set":…}]}}`
behaves differently from `{"fields":{"parent":…}}`, the NOT-RESOLVABLE verdict on 37e7 is wrong.

**AC1 becomes answerable from the run output alone:** a 2xx with an unchanged read-back is
accept-and-ignore; a 4xx is rejection. Neither depends on rebar code being correct.

The probes deliberately DO NOT assert on their own — their results fold into the existing oracles'
failure messages, so they add diagnosis without adding a new way for the suite to go red.

Design note: the update-verb example recorded on this ticket was for the CLEAR case, but the wiring
target is the SET case; the helper was generalised to build `{"set": {"key": …}}` when reparenting
and `{"set": None}` when clearing, so one helper covers both.

Verified on current `gerrit/main`: hygiene 0, ruff clean, mypy 421, 58 live tests collect (unchanged).

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## AC1 IS SETTLED BY THE CAPABILITY MAP: DC returns 2xx AND SILENTLY IGNORES

Capability-map run **30863672922** (Jira DC 8.17.1, Server + Software licensed), raw REST with no
rebar transport in the path:

    PUT /rest/api/2/issue/SCRUM-6 {"fields":{"parent":{"key":"SCRUM-1"}}}  -> HTTP 204   [req-0056]
    GET read-back: SCRUM-6 is STILL parented to SCRUM-5, not SCRUM-1               [req-0058]

**The answer to AC1 is accept-and-ignore, not rejection.** A sub-task reparent reports success and
does nothing. That is the dangerous branch of the two this ticket posed, and it confirms the reading
I argued for over the inbound cell's own "the write succeeded, the index is just lagging"
self-diagnosis — a search-index lag cannot make a direct field read return the old value.

Note the payload shape matters: `{"fields":{"parent":null}}` returns **400** `data was not an
object` [req-0055], while the SET form returns 204-and-ignores. Same field, opposite failure modes.

### What this means for the product

`set_parent`'s sub-task branch writes `fields.parent` and gets a 204. Nothing downstream can tell
that the write did nothing — which is why this surfaced only as an unchanged field in a live oracle.
Any fix must **verify by read-back**, because the status code is a lie here. Declining the write
(as the epic branch does when the field is undiscoverable) is the other honest option.

Evidence ids are in the run's `evidence.json`; the raw request/response for each is recorded there.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## CLAIMED. AC3 is the live branch, and the oracle is written and RED.

The capability map settled AC1: DC **accepts-and-ignores**. So of the two conditional ACs, AC2 ("if DC errors") is dead and **AC3 fires**: `set_parent` must either verify by read-back or decline the sub-task branch.

### Design decision — READ-BACK, not an up-front decline (flagging it, since the AC permits either)

Declining hardcodes a belief about one Jira version into the transport. Read-back states the actual requirement — *the parent must move* — and keeps working unchanged if a future DC honours the write; it also reports what really happened per attempt rather than refusing categorically. It costs one extra GET on a path that is already rare. If the operator prefers the blanket decline, this is a small change to reverse.

**Classification matters as much as the detection.** The raise must be `NotImplementedError`, because `dispatch_one` maps that to `outbound-parent-unrepresentable` and everything else to the RETRYABLE `outbound-parent-failed`. DC ignores this write by design, so a retryable classification would spin forever against a platform that is not going to change its mind. That is its own held-out cell.

### The oracle (7 cells, written before any implementation, verified RED: 4 failed / 3 passed)

Held out from the implementer: the ignored-write raise (naming BOTH the requested and the still-observed parent), the `NotImplementedError` classification, the ignored **CLEAR**, and the epic-link regression guard.

The 3 that pass pre-fix are deliberate and are NOT filler:
 * the positive control (an instance that honours the write must not raise) — without it, a fix that raises unconditionally, or that declines the branch outright, satisfies every negative cell;
 * error propagation (a 503 from the update must surface as itself, not be replaced by "the parent did not move");
 * the **epic-link regression guard** — a read-back that looked for `fields.parent` on a non-sub-task would fail every epic parent and undo 1311/9bb9, the only outbound parent path that actually works on DC.

The double models DC honestly: `applies_writes=False` accepts the update, records it, and leaves the stored parent untouched. The parent is rendered into every `issue()` response as a nested object, so a fix that compares against a fixed snapshot — or that treats the field as a bare string — fails.

### SEQUENCING — deliberately not implemented yet

The fix edits `set_parent`, which change 1331 (465d) **relocates into `_hierarchy.py`**. Writing it against today's `transport.py` would guarantee a conflict with a change that already holds `Verified +1`, and the epic's own rule is that nothing lands in that file until the split does. Implementation waits for 1331 to merge; the oracle does not depend on where the method lives.

AC4 (a live cell proves it) will need a harness run AFTER the fix — run 30867072561, in flight now, does not contain it.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## IMPLEMENTED — Gerrit 1337. Read-back verification, plus TWO STALE DOUBLES the held-out cells exposed.

`set_parent`'s sub-task branch now re-reads the issue after writing and raises `NotImplementedError` when the parent did not move, naming both the requested and the still-observed parent. All 9 oracle cells pass, including the 7 never shown to the implementer. Gates: ruff clean, mypy 429, hygiene 0, raw-git-write 0, **2155 reconciler tests pass**, `_hierarchy.py` 199/800.

### THE FINDING WORTH CARRYING: two committed doubles were indistinguishable from the platform bug

The implementer reported an honest conflict — a strict read-back broke `test_dc_epic_link_parent_39c1.py::test_subtask_parent_still_uses_fields_parent`, whose `_FakeClient` records a parent write but never reflects it. **That double's post-write payload is byte-identical to a DC instance exhibiting this exact bug.** It resolved it in PRODUCTION code, by treating a read-back that does not carry `parent` as 'no evidence' and returning.

**I did not accept that, and the reasoning is the point.** It is defensible in the abstract — a fields-limited projection and a parentless issue are the same absence — but not at THIS call site: the read-back fetches the whole issue with no `fields=` projection, so for a sub-task the key is present whenever a parent is. The branch was unreachable on real DC and existed only to satisfy a double that does not model state. That is production code shaped by a test's limitation, and it reintroduces the silent pass this ticket exists to remove — the same 'we could not check must not read as success' rule I had just written into 3fe5's provisioning assertion hours earlier.

So instead: made the doubles faithful, and made the check strict. **A second stale double surfaced immediately** — `test_dc_live_oracles_discriminate_5200.py::_FakeIssue`, same shape, same problem — which the first fix would have masked entirely.

Both now apply the parent write into their `.raw`, so their cells keep asserting the write SHAPE (their actual subject) rather than failing on persistence. Added two cells: a SET whose read-back shows no parent MUST raise, and its mirror — a CLEAR is satisfied by an absent parent, so 'absent means no parent' is not misread as 'absent always fails'.

**This is session-log finding #2 recurring** (a change makes production call a NEW method on an injected collaborator → every existing double is a candidate vacuous oracle). Here the new call was a second `issue()` read, and TWO doubles were silently wrong. Neither failed to tell me — they failed loudly only because the production check was strict.

### AC status

- [x] AC1 live behaviour established (capability map: 204-and-ignores)
- [x] AC2 dead — DC does not error
- [x] AC3 `set_parent` verifies by read-back rather than silently claiming success
- [ ] AC4 a live cell proves it — needs a harness run CONTAINING 1337; run 30867072561 does not.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## THE READ-BACK FIRES ON A REAL INSTANCE — harness run 30870845838

Both sub-task cells changed their failure mode, and the new one IS the fix working:

    NotImplementedError: set_parent could not move the parent of sub-task 'RBJRSRT-3' on Jira
    Data Center: it asked for 'RBJRSRT-2' and Jira accepted the fields.parent write, but a
    fresh read of the issue still reports 'RBJRSRT-1'. Data Center accepts this write and
    silently ignores it (HTTP 204, field unchanged), so the mutation did not happen and
    retrying the same write cannot make it happen.

Before the fix the same cells reported `fields.parent on X is STILL Y — the silent-no-op signature`, an assertion noticing an unchanged field AFTER the fact. Now the TRANSPORT itself detects the lie and refuses. That message can only be produced by the read-back executing against DC 8.17.1 and finding the mismatch, so the mechanism is live-proven, not unit-proven.

Both cells remain RED, and that is correct: DC genuinely cannot reparent a sub-task. What changed is that the failure is now loud, accurate and attributed instead of being reported as a successful mutation.

### AC4 IS NOT TICKED YET, AND I WANT TO BE PRECISE ABOUT WHY

AC4 asks for 'a live cell PROVES the chosen path'. The evidence above is the read-back firing — but it surfaces as the *error message of two cells whose subject is something else* (that a reparent round-trips), both of which are red for a platform reason. No cell currently has the refusal itself as its subject.

That is a real distinction, and it is the same one I got wrong on [rebar:39c1-2a32-b564-4b4b] earlier tonight by accepting an adjacent green as the claim. I am not repeating it. AC4 needs a cell that asserts `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)` on a sub-task reparent against the live instance — GREEN, with the refusal as its subject, exactly the shape 37e7's rewrite took for its limitation. Writing that cell now; it rides the next harness run.

- [x] AC1 live behaviour established (accept-and-ignore)
- [x] AC2 dead — DC does not error
- [x] AC3 `set_parent` verifies by read-back rather than silently claiming success — **live-proven**
- [ ] AC4 a cell whose SUBJECT is the refusal, green on a live run

compiled_state.description:
# DC sub-task reparent via `PUT fields.parent` is accepted and IGNORED — the parent never moves

## Provenance

Surfaced live by harness run **30834117797** (job 91755000385, main @ `25ead49f3e`), by TWO
independent cells in opposite directions. Not predicted by any ticket; found only because story
5200's repaired cells read the field back instead of trusting the call's return.

## Evidence — two cells, and only one reading survives both

**Outbound (`test_outbound_set_subtask_parent_round_trips`)** — verbatim:

> the outbound parent set: fields.parent on RBJUUVX-3 is STILL 'RBJUUVX-1' — the parent it had
> BEFORE the mutation. Expected 'RBJUUVX-2'. This is the silent-no-op signature: `set_parent`
> writes `fields.parent` for a sub-task (`jira_datacenter/transport.py:711-712`) and every core
> caller swallows its failure (`dispatch_one.py:571-578` warns and continues), so an unchanged
> field is the ONLY place the failure is observable.

**Inbound (`test_inbound_set_subtask_parent_round_trips`)** — timed out after 90s / 45 attempts
waiting for `get_parent_map` to show the reparent; last parent seen was the ORIGINAL.

The inbound cell self-diagnoses as search-index lag ("NOT a bridge defect"). **That reading cannot
account for the outbound cell**, which read `fields.parent` back DIRECTLY over raw REST — no search
index involved — and still saw the pre-mutation value. A lagging index cannot make a direct field
read return stale data. The reading that explains BOTH is that the write itself never took effect.

## Why this matters more than one red cell

`transport.py:688-689` already carries a note that DC may **accept a `PUT {'parent': None}` and
ignore it**. This is the same accept-and-ignore shape on the SET path. If it holds, then the
sub-task branch of `set_parent` — the branch that exists precisely because it is supposed to be the
shape DC accepts — does not work on DC 8.17.1 at all.

That directly undercuts the premise of [rebar:39c1-2a32-b564-4b4b], whose mechanism analysis reads
"the one child shape DC accepts (sub-task)". If the sub-task write is also a no-op, then 39c1's
AC1 ("the emit gate and DC's accepted child shape overlap for at least one real configuration")
cannot be satisfied by the sub-task path, and the Epic Link path added in change 1302 becomes the
ONLY candidate rather than a second one.

## What is NOT yet established

Whether DC returns a success status for the ignored write, or an error that
`dispatch_one.py:571-578` swallows. The two have different fixes and the harness output does not
distinguish them — the swallow is exactly why. 39c1's AC4 alerting change (bridge_alerts entry on
every `set_parent` failure arm) will make the difference visible on the next run: an alert present
means DC errored and we hid it; no alert means DC returned success and lied.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] the live behaviour is established: does DC 8.17.1 return success, or an error, for a
      sub-task `PUT fields.parent` that does not take effect? Recorded with the run id and the
      raw response.
- [ ] if DC errors: the error is surfaced (39c1 AC4) and the caller stops reporting the mutation
      as applied
- [ ] if DC accepts-and-ignores: `set_parent` verifies the write by reading the field back, or the
      sub-task branch is declined the way the epic branch was, rather than silently claiming success
- [ ] a live cell proves the chosen path against the real instance — a unit suite CANNOT settle
      this (changes 1276 and 1288 were both mutation-proven and both wrong in production)
